The graph shrink operator  \( \mathrm{GS}_{k_{1}}^{k_{2}}(\cdot) \)  has several properties which will be useful for computing steiner connectivities. Firstly, applying the operator  \( \mathrm{GS}_{k_{1}}^{k_{2}}(\cdot) \)  preserves the steiner connectivity for all edges in the resulting graph.

Property 1: Given a graph G and two integers  \( k_{1} \leq k_{2} \) , the steiner connectivity of each edge of  \( \mathsf{GS}_{k_{1}}^{k_{2}}(G) \)  when computed in  \( \mathsf{GS}_{k_{1}}^{k_{2}}(G) \)  is the same as that computed in G.
Secondly, the steiner connectivity for all edges of \(\mathsf{GS}_k^k (G)\) is \(k\). For example, all edges in Figure 5 have steiner connectivity 3.
Property 2: Given a graph G and an integer k, every edge of  \( \mathsf{GS}_{k}^{k}(G) \)  has steiner connectivity k.
Thirdly, multiple operations of  \( \mathrm{GS}_{k_{1}}^{k_{2}}(\cdot) \)  can be chained together.

Property 3: Given a graph \(G\) and four integers \(k_1 \leq k_2\) and \(k_3 \leq k_4\) such that \(\max\{k_1, k_3\} \leq \min\{k_2, k_4\}\), we have \(\mathsf{GS}_{k_3}^{k_4}(\mathsf{GS}_{k_1}^{k_2}(G)) = \mathsf{GS}_{\max\{k_1, k_3\}}^{\min\{k_2, k_4\}}(G)\).

Our Divide-and-Conquer Approach: ECo-DC. From Property 2, we know that the steiner connectivities of all edges of \(\mathsf{GS}_k^k (G)\) are \(k\). Moreover, from the definitions of steiner connectivity and the graph shrink operator, we know that all edges whose steiner connectivities are \(k\) will be in \(\mathsf{GS}_k^k (G)\). Thus, to compute steiner connectivities of all edges of \(G\), it suffices to compute \(\mathsf{GS}_k^k (G)\) for \(k\in [1,\delta (G)]\). Instead of naively computing \(\mathsf{GS}_k^k (G)\) independently for each \(k\in [1,\delta (G)]\) which would take \(\mathcal{O}\big(\delta (G)\times \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{KECC}}(G)\big)\) time, we propose a divide-and-conquer approach based on the fact that \(\mathsf{GS}_k^k (G)\) is entirely contained in \(\mathsf{GS}_{k_1}^{k_2}\) if \(k_{1}\leq k\leq k_{2}\).
Algorithm 3: ECo-DC(G)

The pseudocode of our approach is shown in Algorithm 3, denoted ECo-DC. It first computes the degeneracy  \( \delta(G) \)  of G (Line 1), and then invokes procedure Compute-DC with input  \( (G, 1, \delta(G)) \)  to compute the steiner connectivities of all edges (Line 2), while

Line 3 constructs the hierarchy tree and will be discussed in Section 4.2. The input to Compute-DC consists of a graph g and an interval  \( [L, H] \) . If L = H, then the steiner connectivities of all edges of g are set as L (Lines 5–6). Otherwise, an integer M is chosen such that  \( L < M \leq H \)  (Line 8), then the set  \( \phi_{M}(g) \)  of M-ECCs of g is computed (Line 9) and two graphs  \( g_{1} \)  and  \( g_{2} \)  are obtained from g based on  \( \phi_{M}(g) \)  (Line 10), and finally the algorithm continues on  \( g_{1} \)  (Line 11) and on  \( g_{2} \)  (Line 12).

We prove by the following lemma that when initially invoking Compute-DC with graph \(G\) and interval \([1, \delta(G)]\), the graph \(g\) being processed for each recursion with interval \([L, H]\) is \(\mathsf{GS}_L^H(G)\).

Lemma 4.1: For Compute-DC, if the input graph g is  \( \mathsf{GS}_{L}^{H}(G) \) , then the two graphs  \( g_{1} \)  and  \( g_{2} \)  obtained at Line 10 are exactly  \( \mathsf{GS}_{L}^{M-1}(G) \)  and  \( \mathsf{GS}_{M}^{H}(G) \) , respectively.

Based on Lemma 4.1, the recursion tree of invoking Compute-DC with input \((G,1,\delta (G))\) is as shown in Figure 6.
The correctness and time complexity of Algorithm 3 are proved by the two theorems below.
Theorem 4.1: Algorithm 3 correctly computes the steiner connectivity for all edges of G.
Theorem 4.2: The time complexity of Algorithm 3 is  \( \mathcal{O}(h\times\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{KECC}}(G)) \) , where h is the height of the recursion tree in Figure 6.

Near-Optimal Time Complexity. Algorithm 3 correctly computes the steiner connectivities of all edges regardless of the choice of M at Line 8, as long as  \( L < M \leq H \) . Yet, the time complexity of Algorithm 3 would vary for different choices of M. For example, if M is always set as  \( L + 1 \)  or always set as H, then the height of the recursion tree would be  \( \delta(G) \)  and thus the time complexity of Algorithm 3 would be  \( \mathcal{O}(\delta(G) \times \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{KECC}}(G)) \)  on the basis of Theorem 4.2. To make the time complexity as low as possible, we will need to reduce the height of the recursion tree. Thus, we propose to set M as  \( \left\lceil \frac{L+H}{2} \right\rceil \) , and prove in the following theorem that the time complexity of Algorithm 3 then becomes  \( \mathcal{O}\big((\log \delta(G)) \times \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{KECC}}(G)\big) \) .
Theorem 4.3: By setting \(M = \left\lceil \frac{L + H}{2} \right\rceil\), the time complexity of Algorithm 3 is \(O((\log \delta(G)) \times \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{KECC}}(G))\).

Following the above theorem, we set \( M = \left\lceil \frac{L + H}{2} \right\rceil \) in Algorithm 3. The time complexity of ECo-DC, which is \( O\big((\log \delta(G)) \times \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{KECC}}(G)\big) \), is optimal up to a logarithmic factor \( \log \delta(G) \). This is because the time complexity of ECo-decomposition cannot be lower than \( \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{KECC}}(G) \), as ECo-decomposition also implicitly computes the \( k \)-ECCs of \( G \); specifically, the \( k \)-ECCs of \( G \) can be obtained from the hierarchy tree in time linear to the sizes of the \( k \)-ECCs.
